content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a complex, multisystem disease where growth and nutrition play a critical role in lung function and overall survival. Individuals with CF often experience intestinal dysbiosis, which refers to an imbalance in the gut microbiota, as well as intestinal inflammation. Probiotics, which are commercially available over-the-counter, have been proposed as a potential intervention to improve both gut and overall health in this population. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of probiotics in improving health outcomes for children and adults with CF. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, trial registries, and relevant literature up to January 2020 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized trials that assessed probiotics in this population. Cross-over RCTs were included if they had a washout phase, and for those without one, only the first phase of the trial was analyzed. A total of 17 trials were identified, of which 12 RCTs (11 completed and one terminated early) involving 464 participants were included in the analysis. Eight trials focused exclusively on children, while four included both children and adults. The duration of the trials ranged from one to 12 months. Nine trials compared probiotics (seven single-strain and three multi-strain preparations) to placebo, two trials compared synbiotics (multi-strain probiotics combined with prebiotics) to placebo, and one trial compared two different probiotic preparations. The overall risk of bias in the trials was judged to be low, although some trials had high risks of performance, attrition, or reporting bias. Funding sources varied, with some trials supported by grants, others by industry, and some with unknown funding. The combined data from four trials (225 participants) suggested that probiotics might reduce the number of pulmonary exacerbations over a fourto 12-month period, with a mean difference (MD) of -0.32 episodes per participant (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.68 to 0.03; P = 0.07). However, the confidence interval included the possibility of both an increase and a decrease in exacerbations, and the evidence was of low certainty. Two trials (127 participants) found no evidence that probiotics affected the duration of antibiotic therapy during the same time frame. Probiotics were found to reduce levels of fecal calprotectin, a marker of intestinal inflammation, based on data from four trials (177 participants), with an MD of -47.4 µg/g (95% CI -93.28 to -1.54; P = 0.04). However, other biomarkers did not show significant differences between probiotics and placebo. Two trials (91 participants) found no evidence that probiotics affected height, weight, or body mass index (BMI). Similarly, combined data from five trials (284 participants) suggested no difference in lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted, over a threeto 12-month period (MD 1.36%; 95% CI -1.20 to 3.91; P = 0.30). Hospitalization rates also showed no significant difference, based on data from two trials (115 participants) (MD -0.44 admissions per participant; 95% CI -1.41 to 0.54; P = 0.38). One trial (37 participants) assessed health-related quality of life. Parent-reported outcomes favored probiotics (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.87; 95% CI 0.19 to 1.55), but child self-reports did not show a significant effect (SMD 0.59; 95% CI -0.07 to 1.26). Data on gastrointestinal symptoms and intestinal microbial profiles were limited and could not be analyzed comprehensively. Adverse events were reported in four trials and one trial protocol (298 participants). No deaths were reported. One terminated trial (12 participants) documented a severe allergic reaction (severe urticaria) in one participant in the probiotic group. Two trials reported single adverse events (vomiting in one child and diarrhea in another). The estimated number needed to harm for any adverse reaction (serious or not) was 52 people, based on low-certainty evidence. In conclusion, probiotics appear to significantly reduce fecal calprotectin levels in individuals with CF, indicating a potential reduction in intestinal inflammation. However, the clinical significance of this finding remains unclear and requires further investigation. Probiotics may have little to no effect on pulmonary exacerbation rates, lung function, or other health outcomes, but additional evidence is needed to draw firm conclusions. Adverse events associated with probiotics were rare and included vomiting, diarrhea, and allergic reactions. Probiotics may be considered as a therapeutic option for individuals with CF, but given the variability in probiotic formulations and dosages, further well-designed, multicenter RCTs of at least 12 months' duration are necessary to better evaluate their efficacy and safety in this population.
